events.title: Ageing Badly
events.description: ‘Ageing Badly’ challenges assumptions that the goal of one’s later years is to age well or ‘successfully’, a message that, since the 1960s, has become pervasive, naturalised in medicine, social theory, and popular culture. Ageing badly, by contrast, encompasses a range of uncomfortable and idiosyncratic ways in which art works, bodies, artists, and ideas, such as ‘the 1960s’, have aged over time. The language of ageing is deeply entangled with those concerning time, history, and the body—languages that have in turn shaped the field of art history and feminist interventions in the field.

events.description: The dominant paradigm in AI research and development envisions the goal as automation of tasks and entire jobs. But another, comparatively marginalized vision has existed since the beginning of AI — that of augmenting workers and amplifying human potential. events.description: Zeyu Ma will present his FPO "Procedural Generation of Unbounded 3D Scenes" on Friday, September 18, 2026 at 1:30 PM in CS 402.The members of Zeyu’s committee are as follows:Examiners: Jia Deng (Adviser), Felix Heide, Adam FinkelsteinReaders: Zhuang Liu, Qixing Huang (UT Austin)A copy of his thesis is available upon request. Please email gradinfo@cs.princeton.edu if you would like a copy of the thesis.Everyone is invited to attend the talk.Abstract follows below:Synthetic data, meaning images and labels generated by computers, is a promising alternative to collecting datasets in the real world and annotating them manually. Procedural generation, which creates content using algorithms, is an effective way to produce it: compact rules express complex, unbounded geometry; parameters give strong controllability; and unlimited varied instances can be generated automatically.This thesis addresses the challenges that unbounded scenes pose for procedural generation. Such scenes are an essential part of diverse environments, yet existing methods cannot handle them efficiently. Producing images from a procedural scene means extracting a mesh from it, and no uniformly spaced mesh serves an unbounded scene: a spacing fine enough for the geometry near the camera is prohibitively dense in the distance, and one coarse enough for the distance is far too sparse up close.Our contributions are in two parts. The first is an efficient procedural system for unbounded terrain, developed as part of Infinigen and published at CVPR 2023. It represents terrain with pseudo-signed distance functions, which keep only the sign of the true distance and thereby unify height maps, volumetric elements such as caves and rocks, and simulated tiles into one composable representation. The second is mesh extraction for a moving camera, a line of work that led to two papers. OcMesher, published at 3DV 2025,builds a camera-aware octree that is refined only where surfaces are visible and close to some camera, and produces a single static mesh valid for a whole set of camera poses. BinocMesher, published at SIGGRAPH Asia 2025, partitions4D spacetime with a binary-octree and slices the extracted 4D mesh at each timestamp, giving temporally smooth meshes along long camera trajectories. In all of them, detail is allocated against where the camera can see, and the allocation is a property of the coordinate system or data structure.

events.title: CITP Seminar - DARK MANSIONS: AI, Innovation, and Fermat’s Last Theorem
events.description: Yiu, Kosoy, and Gopnik (2024) argue that “Cultural evolution depends on a fine balance between imitation and innovation.” Writing in a world prior to reasoning models, they argued that large language models fall squarely on the imitation side. This paper—focused principally on formal and scientific innovation—proposes a finer-grained, three-tier taxonomy: Tier 1 is transmission, Tier 2 is something new (invention) within a fixed problem formulation, and Tier 3 is framework-generating innovation. Tier 3 requires both historical novelty—a new construction or framework—and functional novelty—a downstream dividend, where the apparatus introduced to solve a problem helps to reorganize later work.We explore Andrew Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem as a case of Tier 3 innovation. Core elements of the proof architecture—especially the R = T modularity-lifting strategy and Taylor–Wiles patching—were not present in the prior mathematical literature. Moreover, the proof apparatus has had substantial downstream impact on number theory and the Langlands program. We consider whether a current frontier AI system trained on pre‑1987 mathematical sources could have produced a Wiles-type proof strategy, and offer reasons for doubt. Broadening the argument beyond the Wiles proof, we analyze three current AI paradigms for AI in mathematics and argue that they do not yet offer clear mechanisms for Tier 3 innovation. We then assess the empirical record of AI-assisted mathematical discovery, including the refutation of the unit-distance conjecture and the proof of the existence of non-sofic groups. We find a growing number of striking Tier 2 achievements, but no evidence yet of Tier 3 innovation. Tier 3 innovation, we propose, depends on three capacities—imagination, judgment, and tenacity, understood functionally as capacities for novel decomposition, structural evaluation, and sustained exploration.Current architectures have not shown these capacities at the scale required for Tier 3 innovation. The paper concludes with reflections on the architectural changes that may be needed for the innovation that comes from what Andrew Wiles vividly describes as stumbling around in “dark mansions.”Bio: Joshua Cohen is a political philosopher. He has written on issues of democratic theory, freedom of expression, religious freedom, political equality, democracy and digital technology, good jobs, and global justice. His books include On Democracy (with Joel Rogers); Democracy and Associations (with Joel Rogers); Philosophy, Politics, Democracy; Rousseau: A Free Community of Equals; and The Arc of the Moral Universe and Other Essays. He is co-editor of the Norton Introduction to Philosophy, now in its third edition. Cohen taught at MIT (1977-2005), Stanford (2005-2014), is currently on the faculty at Apple University, and is Distinguished Senior Fellow in Law, Philosophy, and Political Science at University of California, Berkeley. Cohen held the Romanell-Phi Beta Kappa Professorship in 2002-3; gave the Tanner Lectures at UC Berkeley in 2007; the Comte Lectures at LSE in 2012; and the Annual Lecture on Ethics and AI at Oxford in 2024. He is co-editor-in-chief of Boston Review.This talk will be recorded and livestreamed via Zoom. events.title: CITP Seminar - From AI Innovation to AI Deployment: Building the Institutions for an AI-Driven Economy
events.description: Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than the institutions, workforces, and systems expected to absorb it. The challenge ahead is therefore not only one of technological innovation, but of deployment: how do we translate rapidly evolving capabilities into broad-based economic opportunity, institutional capacity, and public benefit?This talk will explore the New Jersey AI Hub as an emerging model for tackling that challenge. A public-private initiative founded by Princeton University, the State of New Jersey, Microsoft, and CoreWeave, the Hub brings together universities, government, industry, startups, and communities to accelerate AI innovation and adoption. Liat Krawczyk will discuss the Hub’s work across entrepreneurship, workforce development, applied AI, and responsible governance—and the larger question underlying it: what new forms of collaboration and infrastructure are needed when technological change moves faster than any one institution can respond?Bio: Liat Krawczyk is the inaugural executive director of the New Jersey AI Hub, a public-private initiative launched by Princeton University, the State of New Jersey, Microsoft, and CoreWeave to advance AI innovation, adoption, and workforce development.Previously, she served at the U.S. Department of Commerce’s CHIPS Program Office, where she led workforce strategy and child care efforts tied to the nation’s historic investment in semiconductor manufacturing. Earlier, she led innovation initiatives at the New York City Economic Development Corporation, including work spanning cybersecurity, emerging technology, and the care economy, and has built and advised organizations at the intersection of technology, economic development, and public policy.Her work focuses on a central question of technological change: how institutions, industries, and communities can adapt quickly enough to turn innovation into broadly shared economic opportunity.This talk will be livestreamed and recorded.
